# Fast, consistent commit checks

Research date: 2026-09-16. This explanation proposes a direction; it does not report benchmark results or change enforcement.

Commit-guard should validate the same messages with the same version and policy locally and in CI. Its current workflow installs npm dependencies at `latest` and checks out two repositories. Remove runtime installation first. Compare a compiled checker with bundled JavaScript: GitHub documents JavaScript actions as faster than Docker actions, which incur container setup and require Linux. Pure JavaScript actions support hosted Windows, macOS, and Linux. Composite packaging alone provides no speed guarantee. [GitHub action types](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/custom-actions)

GitHub's JavaScript tutorial bundles code and dependencies for distribution. Benchmark this baseline against native, separating setup, retrieval, and validation, including cold local starts. This research establishes no millisecond guarantee. The existing semantic PR action demonstrates bundled JavaScript title checking without application checkout. [Packaging JavaScript actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/create-actions/create-a-javascript-action#commit-tag-and-push-your-action), [Semantic PR action](https://github.com/amannn/action-semantic-pull-request)

Define the rules explicitly. Conventional Commits specifies message structure but does not mandate the trailing-period prohibition or 100-character cap reproduced in commitlint. Our recommendation is to make additional style restrictions explicit policy choices, tested identically in both environments. Cody has selected no header-length limit by default; an explicit repository limit can remain optional. [Conventional Commits specification](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)

Locally, use `commit-msg` for immediate feedback and `pre-push` for outgoing commits. Git supplies each pushed ref's local and remote object IDs, with zero IDs for creation or deletion. Batch the selected messages through one checker invocation. Keep validation offline; missing history must produce an actionable diagnostic rather than silently passing. Hooks remain bypassable, so CI is still needed. These implementation recommendations follow Git's hook contracts. [Git hooks](https://git-scm.com/docs/githooks#_pre_push)

The workflow must first decide what constitutes the deliverable: individual commits or a squash title. `pull_request` defaults to `opened`, `synchronize`, and `reopened`; title validation also needs `edited`. The PR event's default SHA identifies a synthetic merge commit, so commit mode must explicitly select the PR head and intended base. Repositories using merge queues need a separate `merge_group: checks_requested` trigger for required checks, with event-specific commit selection. A push check can cover direct pushes to protected branches, but its result necessarily arrives after the push. [Workflow events](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows)

A required message check should not use changed-file filters: unrelated file paths do not make a commit message exempt, and skipped workflows can leave required checks pending. Repository settings should require the stable check name before merging. That complements local prevention; it cannot stop a local commit. [Required-check troubleshooting](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks)

For title mode, inspect event data without checking out application code. For commit mode, compare API retrieval with fetching only the required Git objects and configuration. Checkout fetches one commit by default; fetching all history is an explicit alternative, not a prerequisite for every check. A shallow range must never silently degrade into checking only HEAD when its base is absent. [Checkout behavior](https://github.com/actions/checkout/blob/main/README.md)

API retrieval needs completeness checks. The PR commit endpoint returns at most 250 commits, even when paginated. The comparison endpoint supports fork networks and paginated comparisons; an unpaginated response is limited to 250 commits. Prefer immutable event SHAs over moving branch names, and fail clearly if the complete range cannot be resolved. [PR commits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/pulls#list-commits-on-a-pull-request), [Comparisons](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits#compare-two-commits)

Cancel obsolete PR runs only when replacements validate the complete current PR. Scope concurrency to the workflow and PR identity. Applying the same cancellation to independent push deltas can lose coverage: the newer push does not necessarily include commits from the canceled check. GitHub concurrency also replaces pending runs by default, so merely disabling running-job cancellation does not preserve every queued delta. This coverage consequence is an inference from the documented scheduling behavior. [Concurrency](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency)

Treat titles, messages, and contributor configuration as untrusted data. Pass messages through action inputs, files, or quoted environment variables instead of interpolating them into shell source. Use minimum read permissions, avoid executing PR code through privileged `pull_request_target`, and pin action/workflow dependencies to full commit SHAs. A data-only policy format avoids executing arbitrary JavaScript configuration. [Secure workflow practices](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use)

Bound retries and respect API rate-limit headers. Test fork PRs, large ranges, force pushes, and missing history before promising fast, complete checks. [REST limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)
